studies.title: A Way Out And Unreckoned Provision
studies.meaning: The instruction is symmetrical, which is the point: keep them well or part from them well, the same word for decency used twice, so a separation is asked to be conducted with the same care as a reconciliation. Witnesses are required and told to testify for God rather than for either party. Then the passage lifts out of its subject altogether. Mindfulness of God is promised an opening, and provision from a direction not counted on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a short surah given over to the ending of marriages. Some reports connect the surah's opening to a particular case in Medina, though the accounts differ over who was involved. What is clear is the setting: a society in which a woman leaving a marriage had no independent standing, and where the details of timing, housing and maintenance decided whether she was destitute.

keyTerms.note: From the root for knowing. It names what a community recognises as right without listing it, so the standard is what any decent person would recognise as fair treatment.
A noun of place from the verb to go out. It names a door rather than a rescue, so what is promised is an opening in a situation rather than the removal of the situation.
From the root for counting and accounting. The provision comes from a column the person had not entered in his own ledger, which is a precise way of saying unforeseen rather than miraculous.
From the same counting root as the phrase above, so the two lines are linked by sound. What is enough for a person is named with the vocabulary of arithmetic rather than of feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A divorced woman in seventh-century Arabia returned to her father or her brothers, and if they were dead or unwilling she had nothing. There was no wage work for women and no property she could hold alone in most cases. The requirement of witnesses put a private decision in front of two men who would remember it, which was the only record a community of that kind could keep.
studies.didYouKnow: The promise in these two ayat is quoted far more often than the subject they belong to. An early companion is reported to have said that if people would only take hold of this one ayah it would be enough for them. Its placement is deliberate: the widest promise in the surah arrives in the middle of instructions about a marriage ending.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a general promise inside a passage about separation says something about where God is expected to act. Not only in prayer or in crisis, but in the arrangements people make when a relationship has failed, which is where behaviour is worst and least observed. The promise itself is carefully worded: an exit and unreckoned provision, not a reversal. And sufficiency is offered to the one who hands the outcome over.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same paired instruction in the longest surah, keeping or parting, with the same standard on both.
Shows provision arriving from an unreckoned direction as a scene rather than a promise.
Puts the same word for sufficiency in the mouths of people under threat, as a reply rather than a promise.

studies.applyIt: Think of a relationship that ended badly, at work or in your family, and ask one question: did you end it in a way you would be willing to have described out loud. If not, there is usually one specific thing still available, a message unsent or an amount unreturned. The passage asks for decency at the exit, which is the part nobody watches.

studies.title: Spend From What You Have
studies.meaning: Two instructions, one for each kind of household, and the wording is careful not to shame the second. The wealthy spend from their capacity; the person whose provision is measured out spends from what he was given. Then a general rule: God does not charge a soul beyond what He has handed it, which makes the demand exactly the size of the means. The passage closes with a promise about sequence rather than about amount.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah about the ending of marriages and the maintenance owed afterwards. The ayah before it concerns housing and nursing arrangements, so this one is addressing men supporting a household they no longer live in. No specific occasion is reported. Medina had households at both ends of the range this ayah describes, and both were listening.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning width and room. Wealth is described as having space rather than having much, so the instruction is to spend out of the room a person has.

A passive from the root for decree and measure. The narrower income is described as portioned rather than as lacking, which removes blame from the person in the same phrase that describes his shortage.

A verb for laying a task on someone that costs them effort. The clause that follows fixes the limit at what was given, so the measure is not human capacity in general but this person's actual holdings.
From a root meaning what is easy and, in older usage, the left hand, the side that does not strain. Both words in the closing promise are indefinite, so an ease is promised rather than the ease.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Income in Medina was seasonal and visible. A man's harvest was known to his neighbours to within a few sacks, and there was no way to conceal a bad year or to exaggerate a good one. That made a rule pegged to means workable and also merciful: nobody could be accused of holding back beyond what the street already knew he had.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states the relation between hardship and ease twice, in two different shapes. Here ease is promised after hardship, in sequence. In a short Meccan surah the wording is different: ease is said to be with hardship, alongside it rather than following it. Classical readers noticed the difference and kept both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah calibrates a demand to a person rather than to a standard, which changes what falling short means for someone poor. It also puts a floor under the poorer man: he is told to spend, not excused from it, so the dignity of contributing is preserved along with the limit. The closing promise then addresses the anxiety the instruction creates, and it is worded as a sequence, which allows the hardship to be real while it lasts.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other shape of the same promise, ease placed alongside hardship rather than after it.
States the same limit in the widest form, closing the longest surah with it.
Gives the same two-tier arrangement in the longest surah, using the same distinction between ample and restricted means.

studies.applyIt: If money is tight, give something small anyway this week, and give it without apology or explanation. The ayah refuses to excuse a person from giving because they have little, and it also refuses to measure them against anyone else. Both halves matter, and most people only apply one of them to themselves.
